content: Enteral feeding tubes for preterm or low birth weight infants can be inserted either through the nose (nasal route) or the mouth (oral route). Nasal placement of feeding tubes has the potential to interfere with respiratory function, while oral placement may lead to a higher likelihood of tube displacement, local irritation, and stimulation of the vagus nerve. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether the nasal or oral route for feeding tube placement has a differential impact on feeding tolerance, growth, development, and the occurrence of adverse events in preterm or low birth weight infants. The search strategy employed was the standard approach used by the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. This included comprehensive searches of databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL up to September 2012, as well as conference proceedings and prior reviews. The review included randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials that directly compared nasal versus oral placement of enteral feeding tubes in preterm or low birth weight infants. Data extraction and trial quality assessment were conducted independently by two reviewers using the standard methods of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group. A fixed-effect model was used to synthesize the data, and results were reported as typical risk ratios (RR), risk differences (RD), and weighted mean differences (WMD). Three studies met the eligibility criteria for this review. Two of these were parallel-group randomized controlled trials (van Someren 1984; Dsilna 2005), and one was a cross-over trial (Bohnhorst 2010). The two parallel-group trials included a total of 88 preterm infants. However, only one of these trials provided data on the primary outcomes specified for this review. This trial did not demonstrate any significant effect on the time required to establish enteral feeding or the time needed to regain birth weight. It is important to note that this trial was underpowered to detect small or moderate effect sizes. The cross-over trial involved 35 very preterm infants and did not identify any statistically significant differences in the incidence of apnoea, oxygen desaturation, or bradycardia during the study period. In conclusion, the available data are insufficient to guide clinical practice regarding the choice between nasal and oral routes for feeding tube placement in preterm or low birth weight infants. A large, well-designed randomized controlled trial is necessary to determine whether the route of feeding tube placement has a meaningful impact on feeding outcomes, growth, development, or the incidence of adverse events in this vulnerable population.
